DataFrame API Reference¶

Practical DataFrame API Reference¶

API Reference Style¶

This page documents the full public DataFrame surface with usage-first examples generated from the current table API.

A¶

add¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame add(self, const DataFrame& other) const

DataFrame add(self, scalar other) const

Parameters¶

other : const DataFrame& Second frame, thread, or scalar operand supplied for binary combination, comparison, alignment, or join-style work.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

This applies arithmetic across the compatible numeric payloads in the current object.

Examples¶

Example 1. Add each compatible numeric cell against another aligned frame.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2, 2, 4}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({110.0, 110.0, 100.0}))},
});

auto out = left.add(right);

id  sales
3   210.0
4   230.0
7   190.0

Example 2. Add each compatible numeric cell against one broadcast scalar value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.add(10);

id  sales  city
11  110.0  Accra
12  130.0  Tema
13  100.0  Kumasi

add_prefix¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame add_prefix(self, std::string_view prefix) const

Parameters¶

prefix : std::string_view Text prefix inserted ahead of the existing label or value.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Prepends the supplied text to every feature name. Row values, row order, and case labels stay unchanged.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.add_prefix("feat_");

df.head():
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

out.head():
feat_id  feat_sales  feat_city
1        100.0       Accra
2        120.0       Tema
3         90.0       Kumasi

aggregate¶

API Signature¶

DataFrameView aggregate(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<SummarySpec> specs, bool render = true) const

Parameters¶

specs : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<SummarySpec> Aggregation specs. Each SummarySpec has output, feature, and op.

`op` supports:
- `Count`: Count observed values in the selected feature.
- `Nunique`: Count distinct observed values.
- `Sum`: Compute the numeric sum.
- `Mean`: Compute the arithmetic mean.
- `Median`: Compute the median.
- `Min`: Compute the minimum.
- `Max`: Compute the maximum.
- `Std`: Compute the standard deviation.
- `Var`: Compute the variance.
- `Prod`: Compute the numeric product.

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

Returns¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Builds a compact summary frame from one or more aggregation specs, so you can inspect computed metrics instead of the full row set.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Accra", "Tema", "Tema"}))},
    {"product", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"A", "B", "A", "B"}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0, 150.0}))},
});

auto out = df.aggregate({{"sales_mean", "sales", pluss::table::DataFrame::SummaryOp::Mean}}, false);

metric       value
sales_mean    115.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • aggregate(...) builds a compact summary frame instead of returning grouped rows.

  • Each SummarySpec chooses an output name, a source feature, and a summary operation.

  • Use this when you want one-row summary output such as totals, means, mins, maxes, or counts.

align_cases¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame align_cases(self, const Thread& new_cases) const

Parameters¶

new_cases : const Thread& Replacement case labels in the exact order you want the rows to follow.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Reorders rows so their case labels match the supplied new_cases order. Every requested case must already exist, and the output case axis is rewritten to that order.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

df = df.with_cases(pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"cs0", "cs1", "cs2"})));
auto new_cases = pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"cs1", "cs0", "cs2"}));
auto out = df.align_cases(new_cases);

df.cases():
["cs0", "cs1", "cs2"]

out.cases():
["cs1", "cs0", "cs2"]

out.head():
id  sales  city
2   120.0  Tema
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • align_cases(new_cases) reorders rows by matching the existing case labels against new_cases.

  • Every requested case label must already exist or the call throws.

  • The output case axis is rewritten to new_cases, so both the row order and the labels now follow that target order.

all¶

API Signatures¶

Thread all(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> features = {}, bool skipna = true) const

Thread all(self, std::int64_t axis, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> features = {}, bool skipna = true) const

Parameters¶

features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Feature name(s) that select the target DataFrame columns for the operation.

skipna : bool When true, missing values are skipped during the reduction. When false, missing state can affect the result.

axis : std::int64_t Axis selector. On DataFrame, 0 usually means rows/cases and 1 means features/columns.

Returns¶

Thread Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Applies all to the current DataFrame object. Use the example and output together to see which part of the object changes and which structure is preserved.

Examples¶

Example 1. Evaluate all down the selected boolean columns.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"passed_math", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({true, true, false}, pluss::codem::ScalarType::Bool))},
    {"passed_lab", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({true, false, false}, pluss::codem::ScalarType::Bool))},
});

auto out = df.all({"passed_math", "passed_lab"}, true);

Example 2. Evaluate all across rows using a selected boolean feature set.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"passed_math", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({true, true, false}, pluss::codem::ScalarType::Bool))},
    {"passed_lab", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({true, false, false}, pluss::codem::ScalarType::Bool))},
});

auto out = df.all(1, {"passed_math", "passed_lab"}, true);

Axis Rules¶

  • axis=0 reduces down the selected boolean features and returns one result per feature.

  • axis=1 reduces across features and returns one result per row.

  • These methods expect boolean features; they are not general numeric reducers.

  • Nullable boolean input requires skipna=true.

assign¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame assign(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<DeriveSpec> specs) const

DataFrame assign(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::pair<std::string, Thread>> assignments) const

Parameters¶

specs : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<DeriveSpec> Collection of structured operation specs. Each element describes one requested summary, derive, transform, group, or placement rule depending on the method.

assignments : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::pair<std::string, Thread>> Collection of (feature_name, thread) pairs used to add or replace several features in one call.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Adds or replaces derived features computed from the current frame. Use this when the new column depends on one or more existing columns.

Examples¶

Example 1. Derive one or more columns inside the call from the current frame state.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.assign({{.feature = "profit", .expr = [](const pluss::table::DataFrame& frame) { return pluss::table::Thread(frame.features("sales").as_series().sub(60)); }}});

id  sales  city    profit
1   100.0  Accra   40.0
2   120.0  Tema    35.0
3    90.0  Kumasi  30.0

Example 2. Attach one or more already-computed threads by name.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.assign({{"profit", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({40.0, 35.0, 30.0}))}});

id  sales  city    profit
1   100.0  Accra   40.0
2   120.0  Tema    35.0
3    90.0  Kumasi  30.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • assign(...) adds new derived features or replaces existing ones without mutating the source frame.

  • Each derived thread must match the frame case count.

  • Use the pair form when you already have the computed thread, and the spec form when the value should be computed from the current frame inside the call.

astype¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame astype(self,  pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::pair<std::string_view, pluss::codem::ScalarType>> feature_dtypes) const

DataFrame astype(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> features, pluss::codem::ScalarType dtype) const

Parameters¶

feature_dtypes : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::pair<std::string_view, pluss::codem::ScalarType>> Collection of (feature_name, dtype) pairs used to cast several existing features to explicit scalar dtypes in one call.

features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Feature name(s) that select the target DataFrame columns for the operation.

dtype : pluss::codem::ScalarType Target scalar dtype used by this conversion overload.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

This changes the semantic or numeric type so later operations route through the correct implementation path.

Examples¶

Example 1. Convert several selected features at once by supplying a feature-to-dtype map.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({{"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"100.0", "120.0", "90.0"}))}});

auto out = df.astype({{"sales", pluss::codem::ScalarType::Float64}});

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Convert one or more selected features to a target numeric Series dtype.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({{"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"100.0", "120.0", "90.0"}))}});

auto out = df.astype({"sales"}, pluss::codem::ScalarType::Float64);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Conversion Rules¶

  • These methods rewrite only the selected features; unselected features are passed through unchanged.

  • Duplicate feature names in the request are ignored after the first occurrence.

  • Unknown or empty feature names throw immediately.

  • astype(...) is the direct numeric-series dtype conversion path, while cast(...) is the broader target-selection route.

at¶

API Signature¶

std::string at(self, std::int64_t row, std::string_view feature_name) const

Parameters¶

row : std::int64_t Zero-based row position used by this overload.

feature_name : std::string_view Name of the target feature to read, rewrite, sort by, or promote to cases.

Returns¶

std::string Rendered string result.

What It Does¶

Fetches one value, member, or slice from the current object without changing the source object.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.at(0, "city");

Accra

Practical Behavior¶

  • at(row, feature) returns one scalar value rendered as text.

  • The row is positional here; it does not look up by case label.

  • Use this for quick single-cell inspection, not for typed column work.

B¶

bfill¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame bfill(self) const

Parameters¶

None

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

This is part of the missing-data cleanup path and is usually applied before summaries, grouping, or export.

Examples¶

auto score = pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({71.0, 0.0, 88.0, 0.0}))
                 .with_validity_mask(pluss::make_series({true, false, true, false}, pluss::codem::ScalarType::Bool));
auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"score", score},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi", "Tamale"}))},
});

auto out = df.bfill();

score  city
71.0   Accra
71.0   Tema
88.0   Kumasi
88.0   Tamale

Practical Behavior¶

  • bfill() runs backward fill feature-by-feature across the full frame.

  • A null value is replaced by the next valid value below it in the same feature.

  • Trailing null runs stay null because there is no later value to pull from.

  • If you want to backward-fill only one feature, apply it at the Thread level and assign it back with set(...) or set_features(...).

Common Pattern¶

gradebook.set("Final Points Grade") =
    gradebook.features("Final Points Grade").bfill();

bottom¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame bottom(self, std::string_view feature, std::int64_t n) const

Parameters¶

feature : std::string_view Name of the source feature used by the operation.

n : std::int64_t Number of rows, entries, or depth items to keep in the preview.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Returns the rows with the smallest values in the selected feature.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.bottom("sales", 2);

id  sales  city
3    90.0  Kumasi
1   100.0  Accra

Practical Behavior¶

  • bottom(feature, n) sorts ascending by feature, keeps nulls last, then returns the first n rows.

  • Because nulls are sorted last, null rows are not chosen unless there are not enough non-null rows to satisfy n.

  • n == 0 returns an empty frame with the same schema.

  • The output keeps the original row payloads and case labels of the selected rows.

Argument Effects¶

  • Small n is useful for “lowest few rows” inspection.

  • Larger n gives you the full ascending slice without writing sort_values(...).head(...) yourself.

Equivalent Expanded Form¶

auto out = df.sort_values({pluss::table::DataFrame::ArrangeSpec{"sales", true, true}})
             .head(5, false);

bucketize¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame bucketize(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Double bins, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Int labels = {}, bool right = true, bool include_lowest = true) const

DataFrame bucketize(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> feature_names, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Double bins, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Int labels = {}, bool right = true, bool include_lowest = true) const

DataFrame bucketize(self, std::string_view feature_name, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Double bins, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Int labels = {}, bool right = true, bool include_lowest = true) const

Parameters¶

bins : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Double Strictly increasing interval edges used to define bucket boundaries.

labels : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Int Optional integer labels assigned to the output buckets. Leave empty to let PlussMic use 0, 1, 2, ....

right : bool When true, intervals are right-closed. When false, they are left-closed and right-open.

include_lowest : bool When true, the first bucket also includes its left edge.

feature_names : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Feature name(s) supplied explicitly for subset, ordering, or axis-replacement operations, depending on the method.

feature_name : std::string_view Name of the target feature to read, rewrite, sort by, or promote to cases.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Buckets numeric Series features into interval labels while preserving the rest of the frame unchanged.

Examples¶

Example 1. Bucketize every compatible numeric column in the frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

std::vector<double> bins{0.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0};
std::vector<std::int64_t> labels{1, 2, 3};
auto out = df.bucketize(bins, labels, true, true);

id  sales  city
1   2      Accra
2   3      Tema
3   1      Kumasi

Example 2. Bucketize several selected numeric columns at once.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

std::vector<double> bins{0.0, 95.0, 110.0, 130.0};
std::vector<std::int64_t> labels{1, 2, 3};
auto out = df.bucketize({"id", "sales"}, bins, labels, true, true);

id  sales  city
1   2      Accra
2   3      Tema
3   1      Kumasi

Example 3. Bucketize one numeric column into interval labels.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

std::vector<double> bins{0.0, 95.0, 110.0, 130.0};
std::vector<std::int64_t> labels{1, 2, 3};
auto out = df.bucketize("sales", bins, labels, true, true);

id  sales  city
1   2      Accra
2   3      Tema
3   1      Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • bucketize(...) delegates to thread-level bucketization only for the selected numeric Series features.

  • Non-selected features pass through unchanged, so this is safe to use on mixed-type frames.

  • The no-feature overload auto-selects every numeric Series feature in the frame.

  • Bucket labels are returned as Int64-backed Thread columns and out-of-range values remain null.

cases¶

API Signatures¶

const Thread& cases(self) const

DataFrame cases(self, std::int64_t row) const

DataFrame cases(self, std::pair<std::int64_t, std::int64_t> row_span) const

Parameters¶

row_span : std::pair<std::int64_t, std::int64_t> Row span given as a (start, stop) pair.

feature_idx : std::size_t Zero-based feature position used by this overload.

Returns¶

const Thread& Value produced by this call.

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

std::string Rendered string result.

What It Does¶

Fetches one value, member, or slice from the current object without changing the source object.

Examples¶

Example 1. Read the current case axis thread.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.cases();

Example 2. Extract one row by case position.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.cases(0);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 3. Extract a contiguous row span by case position.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.cases({0, 2});

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 4. Read one cell by row position and feature index.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.cases(0, 0);

1

Example 5. Read one cell by row position and feature name.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.cases(0, "city");

Accra

Overload Guide¶

  • cases(row) and cases(start, stop) return row slices.

  • cases(row, feature) returns one scalar value from a row/feature intersection.

  • Use cases_series() only when the case axis is actually Series-backed.

cases_series¶

API Signature¶

pluss::Series cases_series(self) const

Parameters¶

None

Returns¶

pluss::Series Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Returns the current case axis as a Series, which is useful when you need the row labels as data.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},

});

[0, 1, 2]

cast¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame cast(self,  pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::pair<std::string_view, pluss::codem::ScalarType>> feature_dtypes) const

DataFrame cast(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<CastSpec> specs) const

Parameters¶

feature_dtypes : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::pair<std::string_view, pluss::codem::ScalarType>> Collection of (feature_name, dtype) pairs used to cast several existing features to explicit scalar dtypes in one call.

specs : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<CastSpec> Collection of structured operation specs. Each element describes one requested summary, derive, transform, group, or placement rule depending on the method.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

This changes the semantic or numeric type so later operations route through the correct implementation path.

Examples¶

Example 1. Cast selected features into another Pluss payload family.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({{"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"100.0", "120.0", "90.0"}))}});

auto out = df.astype({{"sales", pluss::codem::ScalarType::Float64}});

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Cast selected features with explicit target-family and dtype control.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({{"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"100.0", "120.0", "90.0"}))}});

auto out = df.cast({{.feature = "sales", .target = pluss::table::ThreadCastTarget::Series, .series_dtype = pluss::codem::ScalarType::Float64}});

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Conversion Rules¶

  • These methods rewrite only the selected features; unselected features are passed through unchanged.

  • Duplicate feature names in the request are ignored after the first occurrence.

  • Unknown or empty feature names throw immediately.

  • astype(...) is the direct numeric-series dtype conversion path, while cast(...) is the broader target-selection route.

cloc¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame cloc(self, std::int64_t row) const

DataFrame cloc(self, std::int64_t start, std::int64_t stop) const

Parameters¶

row : std::int64_t Zero-based row position used by this overload.

start : std::int64_t Inclusive starting position of the slice.

stop : std::int64_t Exclusive ending position of the slice.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Applies cloc to the current DataFrame object. Use the example and output together to see which part of the object changes and which structure is preserved.

Examples¶

Example 1. Select one row by case position.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.cloc(1);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Select a contiguous row slice by case position.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.cloc(0, 2);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • cloc(...) is the case-axis row slice helper.

  • It is equivalent to slicing rows, not selecting by feature names.

  • Use it when you want row-position access in a method that reads like case-location.

combine¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame combine(self, const DataFrame& other) const

DataFrame combine(self, const DataFrame& other, const CombineSpec& spec) const

Parameters¶

other : const DataFrame& Second frame, thread, or scalar operand supplied for binary combination, comparison, alignment, or join-style work.

spec : const CombineSpec& Structured reorder description. It lets you move a subset of features to the front, back, or relative to one anchor feature without listing the entire schema.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Combines this frame with another frame according to the supplied combine policy, such as feature-wise update or join-like alignment.

Examples¶

Example 1. Combine two aligned frames with the default feature-wise policy.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"cost", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({60.0, 80.0, 55.0}))},
});

auto out = left.combine(right);

id  sales  cost
1   100.0  60.0
2   120.0  80.0
3    90.0  55.0

Example 2. Combine two aligned frames with an explicit combine-policy object.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"cost", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({60.0, 80.0, 55.0}))},
});

pluss::table::DataFrame::CombineSpec spec;
spec.op = pluss::table::DataFrame::CombineOp::Update;
auto out = left.combine(right, spec);

id  sales  cost
1   100.0  60.0
2   120.0  80.0
3    90.0  55.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • combine(...) is the lower-level composition route behind feature-wise join/update behaviors.

  • Collision handling depends on the chosen CombineSpec and suffix settings.

  • Use the dedicated helpers such as join(...), update(...), or unify(...) when they fit; use combine(...) when you need explicit combine policy control.

compare¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame compare(self, const DataFrame& other) const

DataFrame compare(self, scalar other) const

Parameters¶

other : const DataFrame& Second frame, thread, or scalar operand supplied for binary combination, comparison, alignment, or join-style work.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

This produces a comparison-style result you can inspect directly or reuse as a mask.

Examples¶

Example 1. Run the not-equal comparison alias against another aligned frame.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2, 2, 4}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({110.0, 110.0, 100.0}))},
});

auto out = left.compare(right);

id  sales
1   true
2   true
3   false

Example 2. Run the not-equal comparison alias against one broadcast scalar value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.compare(10);

id  sales
1   true
2   true
3   false

Practical Behavior¶

  • compare(...) is the “not equal” comparison alias on DataFrame.

  • It returns a boolean-like frame you can inspect directly or reuse as a mask.

  • Use eq/ne/lt/le/gt/ge when you want the comparison intent spelled out directly.

conform_to¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame conform_to(self, const DataFrame& other) const

Parameters¶

other : const DataFrame& Second frame, thread, or scalar operand supplied for binary combination, comparison, alignment, or join-style work.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Reorders and aligns this frame so it is compatible with another frame for downstream joins or arithmetic.

Examples¶

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"cost", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({60.0, 80.0, 55.0}))},
});

auto out = left.conform_to(right);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • conform_to(other) first reorders features to match other.feature_names() and then aligns the case axis to other.cases().

  • Both frames must have the same feature count and the same feature name set.

  • Use this before arithmetic or updates when structure compatibility matters more than preserving the current order.

});

  • copy() gives you a detached frame value for downstream edits.

  • Use it when you want to make the independence of the result explicit in user code or examples.

corr¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrameView corr(self, bool render = false) const

DataFrameView corr(self, CorrMethod method, bool render = false) const

DataFrameView corr(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> features, bool render = false) const

DataFrameView corr(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> features, CorrMethod method, bool render = false) const

Parameters¶

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

method : CorrMethod Correlation method.

Supported values:
- `Pearson`: Ordinary linear correlation.
- `Spearman`: Rank correlation.
- `KendallTau`: Rank-concordance correlation.

features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Feature name(s) that select the target DataFrame columns for the operation.

Returns¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Applies corr to the current DataFrame object. Use the example and output together to see which part of the object changes and which structure is preserved.

Examples¶

Example 1. Find the correlation across all numeric columns using the default correlation method.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.corr(false);

feature  id      sales
id       1.0000  0.3273
sales    0.3273  1.0000

Example 2. Find the correlation across all numeric columns using a non-default correlation method.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.corr(pluss::table::DataFrame::CorrMethod::Spearman, false);

feature  id      sales
id       1.0000  0.3273
sales    0.3273  1.0000

Example 3. Find the correlation for a selected subset of numeric columns.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.corr({"id", "sales"}, false);

feature  id      sales
id       1.0000  0.3273
sales    0.3273  1.0000

Example 4. Find the correlation between selected columns using a non-default correlation method.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.corr({"id", "sales"}, pluss::table::DataFrame::CorrMethod::KendallTau, false);

feature  id      sales
id       1.0000  0.3273
sales    0.3273  1.0000

Practical Behavior¶

  • corr(...) builds a correlation matrix across numeric features only.

  • If you do not pass a feature list, the method auto-selects numeric features from the frame.

  • Supported methods route through thread-level correlation kernels such as Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall Tau.

count¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrameView count(self, bool render = true) const

Returns a size/count summary for the current object without changing it.

Examples¶

Example 1. Compute count for each numeric column in the frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({

sales    3

Example 2. Compute count across rows instead of returning one summary value per numeric column.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.count(1);

feature  value
id       3
sales    3
city     3

Example 3. Compute count across rows instead of returning one summary value per numeric column.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.count(static_cast<std::int64_t>(1));

feature  value
id       3
sales    3
city     3

Practical Behavior¶

  • count() returns per-feature non-null counts as a summary frame.

  • This is not row count; use nrows() when you want total case count.

count_by¶

API Signature¶

DataFrameView count_by(self, std::string_view feature, std::int64_t top_n = 0, bool dropna = true, bool render = true) const

Parameters¶

feature : std::string_view Name of the source feature used by the operation.

top_n : std::int64_t Optional cap on how many grouped rows to keep after sorting. Use 0 to keep every group.

dropna : bool When true, null grouping keys or null values are excluded where the method supports that policy. When false, null participates instead of being removed.

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

Returns¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Groups by one feature and returns per-group row counts.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Accra", "Tema", "Tema"}))},
    {"product", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"A", "B", "A", "B"}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0, 150.0}))},
});

auto out = df.count_by("city", 3, true, false);

city    count
Accra   2
Tema    2

Practical Behavior¶

  • count_by(feature, ...) groups by one feature, counts rows per distinct value, sorts by count descending, then trims to top_n when requested.

  • Ties are broken by key name in ascending order.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({

3

Practical Behavior¶

  • count_null_rows() counts how many rows contain at least one null value anywhere in the frame.

  • Use this as a quick completeness check before grouping, joining, or export.

describe¶

API Signature¶

DataFrameView describe(self, bool render = true) const

Parameters¶

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

Returns¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Returns descriptive summary statistics for the selected numeric features.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.describe(false);

feature  count  mean   min   max
sales    3      103.3  90.0  120.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • describe() summarizes numeric series features only.

  • Non-numeric and non-series features are skipped rather than coerced.

  • Null values are removed before the statistics are computed.

});

0.2  12.0  Tema
0.3   9.0  Kumasi

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({

});

  • drop(...) removes features, not rows.

dropna¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame dropna(self) const

Parameters¶

None

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

This is part of the missing-data cleanup path and is usually applied before summaries, grouping, or export.

Examples¶

auto sales = pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 0.0, 90.0}))
                 .with_validity_mask(pluss::make_series({true, false, true}, pluss::codem::ScalarType::Bool));
auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3})},
    {"sales", sales},
    {"city", pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"})},
});

auto out = df.dropna();

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • dropna() removes rows that contain at least one null value anywhere in the frame.

  • Use dropna_all(features) when the rule should apply only to selected features and only when all of them are null.

dropna_all¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame dropna_all(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> features = {}) const

Parameters¶

features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Feature name(s) that select the target DataFrame columns for the operation.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

This is part of the missing-data cleanup path and is usually applied before summaries, grouping, or export.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.dropna_all({"sales"});

id  sales
2   null
3   90.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • dropna_all(features) removes rows only when all selected features are null in that row.

  • Rows with at least one observed value among the selected features are kept.

value : const char* Replacement, fill, or write value used by mutation-style methods such as put(...), fillna(...), or replace(...).

Returns¶

DataFrame& Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

This is part of the missing-data cleanup path and is usually applied before summaries, grouping, or export.

Examples¶

Example 1. Fill missing values in place with a text scalar.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({{"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))}});

df.fillna_("Unknown");

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Fill missing values in place with a TimeIndex scalar.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({{"idx", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_timeindex({"2024-01-01T09:10:00Z", "2024-01-01T09:40:00Z"}))}});

df.fillna_(pluss::make_timeindex("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z"));

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 3. Fill missing values in place with a Timeline scalar.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({{"ts", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_timeline({"2024-01-01T09:10:00Z", "2024-01-01T09:40:00Z"}))}});

df.fillna_(pluss::make_timeline("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z"));

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 4. Fill missing values in place with a numeric scalar.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

df.fillna_(0.0);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 5. Fill missing values in place with a text scalar.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({{"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))}});

df.fillna_("Unknown");

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

DataFrame filter(self, const pluss::Series& bool_mask) const

DataFrame filter(self, const Thread& bool_mask) const

Parameters¶

bool_mask : const pluss::Series& Boolean row mask. true keeps or rewrites the corresponding row, while false leaves it out or leaves the original value unchanged depending on the method.

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Keeps only the rows where the supplied boolean mask is true.

Examples¶

Example 1. Filter rows using an explicit boolean Series mask.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto mask = pluss::make_series({true, false, true}, pluss::codem::ScalarType::Bool);
auto out = df.filter(mask);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Filter rows using a boolean mask built from an existing frame expression.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto mask = df.features("sales") >= 95.0;
auto out = df.filter(mask);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

group_by¶

API Signature¶

DataFrameView group_by(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> keys, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<GroupSpec> specs, bool dropna_keys = true, bool render = true) const

Parameters¶

keys : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Feature names whose distinct value combinations define the output groups.

specs : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<GroupSpec> Grouped aggregation specs. Each GroupSpec has output, feature, and op.

`op` supports:
- `Count`: Count observed values inside each group.
- `Nunique`: Count distinct observed values inside each group.
- `Sum`: Compute the numeric sum inside each group.
- `Mean`: Compute the arithmetic mean inside each group.
- `Min`: Compute the minimum inside each group.
- `Max`: Compute the maximum inside each group.

dropna_keys : bool When true, rows with null pivot/group keys are excluded before reshaping.

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

Returns¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Groups rows by one or more key features and computes the requested aggregations for each group.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Accra", "Tema", "Tema"}))},
    {"product", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"A", "B", "A", "B"}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0, 150.0}))},
});

auto out = df.group_by({"city"}, {{"sales_sum", "sales", pluss::table::DataFrame::GroupOp::Sum}}, true, false);

city    sales_sum
Accra   220.0
Tema    240.0

    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2, 2, 4}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({110.0, 110.0, 100.0}))},
});

auto out = left.le(right);

id  sales
1   true
2   true
3   false

Example 2. Compare each compatible cell using the <= relation against one broadcast scalar value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.le(10);

id  sales
1   true
2   true
3   false

load¶

API Signatures¶

static DataFrame load(std::string_view source_type, std::string_view filepath)

static DataFrame load(std::string_view source_type, std::string_view filepath, char sep, std::optional<std::size_t> ncases = std::nullopt, std::vector<std::string> usefeats = {}, std::optional<std::string> case_col = std::nullopt, pluss::loader::BadLinePolicy on_bad_lines = pluss::loader::BadLinePolicy::Error)

static DataFrame load(std::string_view source_type, std::string_view filepath, char sep, std::optional<std::size_t> ncases, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> usefeats, std::optional<std::string> case_col = std::nullopt, pluss::loader::BadLinePolicy on_bad_lines = pluss::loader::BadLinePolicy::Error)

static DataFrame load(std::string_view source_type, std::string_view filepath, const pluss::loader::Config& config)

static DataFrame load(std::string_view source_type, std::string_view filepath, const pluss::loader::ReadCsvOptions& options)

static DataFrame load(std::string_view source_type, std::string_view filepath, std::initializer_list<pluss::loader::ConfigEntry> config_entries)

Parameters¶

source_type : std::string_view Storage format selector such as "csv", "xlsx", "json", or "parquet".

filepath : std::string_view File location to read from or write to. Use a neutral project path such as path/to/data.csv.

sep : char Column separator used for delimited text files such as CSV.

ncases : std::optional<std::size_t> Optional row limit applied while loading. Leave unset to read the whole source.

usefeats : std::vector<std::string> Feature names to load from the source. Leave empty to load every available feature.

case_col : std::optional<std::string> Optional source column that should become the DataFrame case axis while loading.

on_bad_lines : pluss::loader::BadLinePolicy Malformed-line policy for delimited input.

Supported values:
- `Error`: Stop immediately when a malformed row is encountered.
- `Warn`: Continue while reporting the malformed row.
- `Skip`: Ignore malformed rows silently.

config : const pluss::loader::Config& Loader or saver configuration object. Use this when you want to pass a prebuilt option bundle instead of positional arguments.

options : const pluss::loader::ReadCsvOptions& Typed loader, renderer, SQL, plotting, or policy options for this overload.

config_entries : std::initializer_list<pluss::loader::ConfigEntry> Inline configuration entries used to build a lightweight loader configuration without naming a separate config object.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Loads the object from disk using the corresponding PlussMic loader route.

Examples¶

Example 1. Load a runtime-selected source type with the default reader for that format.

auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::load("csv", "path/to/data.csv");

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Load a runtime-selected delimited source while overriding the separator, row limit, and projected feature list.

auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::load("csv", "path/to/data.csv", ',', 8, std::vector<std::string>{"Agency Name", "State"}, std::nullopt);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 3. Load a runtime-selected delimited source while projecting only a selected feature subset from a lightweight string view.

std::array<std::string_view, 2> usefeats{"Agency Name", "State"};
auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::load("csv", "path/to/data.csv", ',', 8, usefeats, std::nullopt);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 4. Load a runtime-selected source type with a reusable loader configuration object.

pluss::loader::Config config{
    {"ncases", 8},
    {"features", {"Agency Name", "State"}},
};
auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::load("csv", "path/to/data.csv", config);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 5. Load a delimited file through the format-switched entry point while controlling parsing with a typed CSV options object.

pluss::loader::ReadCsvOptions options;
options.ncases = 8;
options.case_col = "Agency Name";
auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::load("csv", "path/to/data.csv", options);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 6. Load a runtime-selected source type while passing inline loader configuration entries.

auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::load("csv", "path/to/data.csv", {
    {"ncases", 8},
    {"features", {"Agency Name", "State"}},
});

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • load(...) is the format-switched entry point behind the explicit file loaders.

  • Use it when the source format is chosen at runtime; otherwise, the format-specific loader is clearer.

  • CSV-style overloads let you control separator, row limits, feature projection, case-axis promotion, and bad-line policy.

Practical Behavior¶

  • load_csv(...) loads one external source into typed PlussMic columns.

  • Positional overloads are quick for ad-hoc work, while option/config overloads are better when you want repeatable loader settings.

std::vector<std::int64_t> sheets{0, 1};

Example 8. Load several worksheets by name from a standard string container.

std::vector<std::string> sheets{"Sheet 1", "Sheet 2"};

Sheet1 -> [3 cs x 3 feat]
Sheet2 -> [3 cs x 3 feat]

Example 9. Load several worksheets by zero-based sheet index from a lightweight integer view.

std::array<std::int64_t, 2> sheets{0, 1};
auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::load_excel("path/to/data.xlsx", sheets, true);

Sheet1 -> [3 cs x 3 feat]
Sheet2 -> [3 cs x 3 feat]

Example 10. Load several worksheets by name from a lightweight string view.

std::array<std::string_view, 2> sheets{"Sheet 1", "Sheet 2"};
auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::load_excel("path/to/data.xlsx", sheets, true);

Sheet1 -> [3 cs x 3 feat]
Sheet2 -> [3 cs x 3 feat]

Example 11. Load several worksheets by zero-based sheet index using an inline integer list.

auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::load_excel("path/to/data.xlsx", {0, 1}, true);

Sheet1 -> [3 cs x 3 feat]
Sheet2 -> [3 cs x 3 feat]

Example 12. Load several worksheets by name using an inline list of sheet labels.

auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::load_excel("path/to/data.xlsx", {"Sheet 1", "Sheet 2"}, true);

Sheet1 -> [3 cs x 3 feat]
Sheet2 -> [3 cs x 3 feat]

Example 13. Load every worksheet from an Excel workbook into one multi-sheet load bundle.

auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::load_excel("path/to/data.xlsx", nullptr, true);

Sheet1 -> [3 cs x 3 feat]
Sheet2 -> [3 cs x 3 feat]

Practical Behavior¶

  • load_excel(...) loads one external source into typed PlussMic columns.

  • Positional overloads are quick for ad-hoc work, while option/config overloads are better when you want repeatable loader settings.

  • Excel multi-sheet overloads return pluss::loader::LoadResult because several frames may be produced at once.

lt¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame lt(self, const DataFrame& other) const

DataFrame lt(self, scalar other) const

Parameters¶

other : const DataFrame& Second frame, thread, or scalar operand supplied for binary combination, comparison, alignment, or join-style work.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

This produces a comparison-style result you can inspect directly or reuse as a mask.

Examples¶

Example 1. Compare each compatible cell using the < relation against another aligned frame.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2, 2, 4}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({110.0, 110.0, 100.0}))},
});

auto out = left.lt(right);

id  sales
1   true
2   false
3   true

Example 2. Compare each compatible cell using the < relation against one broadcast scalar value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.lt(110);

id  sales
1   true
2   false
3   true

Comparison Rules¶

  • lt(...) returns a boolean-style frame with the same case axis and selected feature layout as the input.

  • Scalar/native comparisons broadcast the right-hand value across every compatible numeric cell.

  • Frame-vs-frame comparisons are row-wise and require compatible shape and feature alignment.

M¶

matrix¶

API Signature¶

MatrixValues matrix(self) const

Parameters¶

None

Returns¶

MatrixValues Grouped matrix blocks split by payload family (Series, Note, Timeline, and TimeIndex).

What It Does¶

Packs same-kind features into matrix-shaped pluss blocks so lower-level numeric, text, or temporal kernels can consume them efficiently.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto blocks = df.matrix();
auto out = fmt::format(
    "series blocks: {}\nnote blocks: {}\ntimeline blocks: {}\ntimeindex blocks: {}",
    blocks.series_span().size(),
    blocks.note_span().size(),
    blocks.timeline_span().size(),
    blocks.timeindex_span().size());

series blocks: 1
note blocks: 1
timeline blocks: 0
timeindex blocks: 0

Practical Behavior¶

  • matrix() does not coerce every feature into one mixed block.

  • Instead, it packs features by payload family so numeric, note, timeline, and timeindex data stay type-stable.

  • Use as_series(), as_note(), as_timeline(), or as_timeindex() only when the frame contributes exactly one block of that family.

mod¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame mod(self, const DataFrame& other) const

DataFrame mod(self, scalar other) const

Parameters¶

other : const DataFrame& Second frame, thread, or scalar operand supplied for binary combination, comparison, alignment, or join-style work.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

This applies arithmetic across the compatible numeric payloads in the current object.

Examples¶

Example 1. Compute the modulus of each compatible numeric cell against another aligned frame.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2, 2, 4}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({110.0, 110.0, 100.0}))},
});

auto out = left.mod(right);

id  sales
1   100.0
0    10.0
3    90.0

Example 2. Compute the modulus of each compatible numeric cell against one broadcast scalar value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.mod(10);

id  sales  city
1   0.0    Accra
2   0.0    Tema
3   0.0    Kumasi

notna¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame notna(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> features = {}) const

Parameters¶

features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Feature name(s) that select the target DataFrame columns for the operation.

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

This is part of the missing-data cleanup path and is usually applied before summaries, grouping, or export.

Examples¶

auto sales = pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 0.0, 90.0}))
                 .with_validity_mask(pluss::make_series({true, false, true}, pluss::codem::ScalarType::Bool));

});

auto out = df.notna({"sales"});

sales
true
false
true

Practical Behavior¶

  • notna(...) returns a boolean-style frame marking which cells are observed rather than missing.

  • Use it to build masks before filter(...), replacement policies, or diagnostic summaries.

  • notna(...) and notnull(...) are equivalent.

Parameters¶

name : std::string Feature name to insert or move.

feature : const Thread& Full thread payload to insert at the target position. Its length must match the frame case count.

anchor_feature : std::string_view Reference feature used to place a newly inserted or moved feature before or after an existing column.

after : bool When false, placement happens before the anchor. When true, placement happens after the anchor.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Moves one existing feature relative to an anchor feature, or inserts a brand-new feature directly before or after that anchor.

Examples¶

Example 1. Insert a new feature relative to an anchor feature without rebuilding the whole schema.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.place("profit", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({40.0, 35.0, 30.0})), "sales", true);

id  sales  profit  city
1   100.0  40.0    Accra
2   120.0  35.0    Tema
3    90.0  30.0    Kumasi

Example 2. Move one existing feature relative to an anchor feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.place("city", "id", false);

city    id  sales
Accra   1   100.0
Tema    2   120.0
Kumasi  3    90.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • place(name, feature, anchor, after) inserts a brand-new feature relative to an existing anchor.

  • place(name, anchor, after) moves an existing feature without forcing you to restate the full feature order.

  • When after=false, placement happens before the anchor. When after=true, placement happens after the anchor.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},

});

Applies plot3d to the current DataFrame object. Use the example and output together to see which part of the object changes and which structure is preserved.

Example 1. Create the 3D plotting accessor with default plot options.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"x", pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0})},
    {"y", pluss::make_series({4.0, 3.0, 2.0})},
    {"z", pluss::make_series({2.0, 5.0, 4.0})},
});

auto fig = df.plot3d().scatter("x", "y", "z");

Figure(scatter3d/line3d)

Example 2. Create the 3D plotting accessor with an explicit plot-options object.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"x", pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0})},
    {"y", pluss::make_series({4.0, 3.0, 2.0})},
    {"z", pluss::make_series({2.0, 5.0, 4.0})},
});

pluss::table::DataFramePlotOptions options;
options.width = 900.0;
auto fig = df.plot3d(options).scatter("x", "y", "z");

Figure(scatter3d/line3d)

pow¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame pow(self, const DataFrame& other) const

DataFrame pow(self, scalar other) const

Parameters¶

other : const DataFrame& Second frame, thread, or scalar operand supplied for binary combination, comparison, alignment, or join-style work.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

This applies arithmetic across the compatible numeric payloads in the current object.

Examples¶

Example 1. Raise each compatible numeric cell against another aligned frame.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0, 4.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({3.0, 2.0, 5.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({3.0, 2.0, 1.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0, 2.0}))},
});

auto out = left.pow(right);

a    b
8.0  9.0
9.0  8.0
4.0  25.0

Example 2. Raise each compatible numeric cell against one broadcast scalar value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.pow(2);

a    b
1.0  4.0
4.0  16.0
9.0  25.0

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({

});

auto stmt = df.prepare_sql("SELECT id, sales FROM self WHERE sales > {min_sales}");

Example 2. Prepare a parameterized SQL statement with an explicit SQL options object.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},

});

SQL accessor / prepared statement created

prod¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrameView prod(self, bool render = true) const

Thread prod(self, int axis, bool skipna = true) const

Thread prod(self, std::int64_t axis, bool skipna = true) const

Parameters¶

render : bool When true, the summary view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want the summary object without implicit display.

axis : int Reduction axis. 0 computes one product per numeric feature, while 1 computes one product per row across numeric features.

skipna : bool When true, missing values are skipped during the reduction. When false, missing state can affect the result.

Returns¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

Thread Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Computes per-feature or per-row products across numeric data.

Examples¶

Example 1. Compute one product per numeric feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.prod(false);

feature  value
a        6.0
b        40.0

Example 2. Compute products across rows instead of returning one product per numeric feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.prod(1, true);

[2.0, 8.0, 15.0]

Example 3. Compute products across rows instead of returning one product per numeric feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.prod(1, true);

[2.0, 8.0, 15.0]

Axis Rules¶

  • prod(render=false) returns a compact summary view with one product per numeric feature.

  • prod(axis=0) returns a numeric thread with one product per numeric feature.

  • prod(axis=1) returns a numeric thread with one product per row across numeric features.

API Signatures¶

Parameters¶

feature : std::string_view Feature name to rewrite.

bool_mask : const pluss::Series& Boolean row mask. true keeps or rewrites the corresponding row, while false leaves it out or leaves the original value unchanged depending on the method.

value : const char* Replacement scalar, string, null, or thread written only where the mask is true.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Writes a replacement value only where a boolean mask is true and returns the updated frame.

Examples¶

Example 1. Rewrite selected rows using a boolean Series mask and a text literal as the replacement value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto mask = pluss::make_series({false, true, false}, pluss::codem::ScalarType::Bool);
auto out = df.put("city", mask, "Tamale");

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   999.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Rewrite selected rows using a boolean Series mask and another full Thread as the replacement values.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto mask = pluss::make_series({false, true, false}, pluss::codem::ScalarType::Bool);
auto repl = pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({500.0, 999.0, 500.0}));
auto out = df.put("sales", mask, repl);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   999.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • put(feature, mask, value) rewrites only the rows where the mask evaluates true.

  • The mask must match the frame case count.

  • Use put(...) when you want a new frame result, and put_(...) when you want the same rewrite in place.

    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto mask = df.features("id") == 2.0;
df.put_("sales", mask, 999.0);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tamale
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 10. Rewrite rows in place using a boolean Thread mask and a text literal as the replacement value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto mask = df.features("id") == 2.0;
df.put_("city", mask, std::string_view("Tamale"));

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tamale
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • put_(feature, mask, value) rewrites only the rows where the mask evaluates true.

  • The mask must match the frame case count.

  • Use put(...) when you want a new frame result, and put_(...) when you want the same rewrite in place.

Q¶

query¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame query(self, std::string_view expression) const

Parameters¶

expression : std::string_view Boolean filter expression written against feature names, such as "sales > 95" or "city == \"Accra\"". Rows where the expression evaluates true are kept.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Keeps only the rows that satisfy the supplied filter expression or mask-producing query.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.query("sales > 95");

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema

Practical Behavior¶

  • query(expression) keeps rows where the expression evaluates true.

  • Feature names are referenced directly inside the expression string.

  • String comparisons should use quoted values, especially when feature names contain spaces.

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

Builds a new case axis from the supplied labels and aligns rows onto that case order.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

df = df.with_cases(pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"cs0", "cs1", "cs2"})));
auto cases = pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"cs1", "cs0", "cs2"}));
auto out = df.reindex_cases(cases);

df.cases():
["cs0", "cs1", "cs2"]

out.cases():
["cs1", "cs0", "cs2"]

out.head():
id  sales  city
2   120.0  Tema
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

reorder¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame reorder(self, const ReorderSpec& spec) const

DataFrame reorder(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> names) const

Parameters¶

spec : const ReorderSpec& Structured reorder description. It lets you move a subset of features to the front, back, or relative to one anchor feature without listing the entire schema.

names : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Collection of feature, slot, or stream names supplied in positional order.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Moves selected features into a new relative position while preserving row data and the untouched feature order.

Examples¶

Example 1. Move selected features with an explicit partial-order spec.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

pluss::table::DataFrame::ReorderSpec spec;
spec.features = {"sales"};
spec.placement = pluss::table::DataFrame::ReorderPlacement::After;
spec.anchor = "city";
auto out = df.reorder(spec);

id  city    sales
1   Accra   100.0
2   Tema    120.0
3   Kumasi   90.0

Example 2. Move selected features together while preserving the relative order of everything else.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.reorder({"city"});

city    id  sales
Accra   1   100.0
Tema    2   120.0
Kumasi  3    90.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • reorder({"a", "b"}) now means “move these features together and preserve the relative order of everything else.”

  • Use ReorderSpec when you need to move a subset to the front, back, before an anchor, or after an anchor.

  • This avoids listing a 3000-feature schema just to reposition two columns.

Parameters¶

from : const char* Value to search for inside the selected compatible features. Its type decides which feature kinds participate.

to : const char* Replacement value written anywhere from matches. Use pluss::null when you want matched cells to become missing.

features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Optional feature subset. Leave empty to apply the replacement across every compatible feature of the relevant kind.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Replaces matched scalar or pluss-typed values across selected compatible features and returns the updated frame.

Examples¶

Example 1. Work with a selected feature subset.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"midterm_1", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({0.0, 12.0, 0.0}))},
    {"midterm_2", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({8.0, 0.0, 15.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Tema"}))},
});

auto out = df.replace("Tema", "Tamale", {"city"});

midterm_1  midterm_2  city
0.0        8.0        Accra
12.0       0.0        Tamale
0.0        15.0       Tamale

Practical Behavior¶

  • replace(from, to, features) dispatches by value type, so numeric replacements touch numeric series features while string replacements touch note features.

  • If features is empty, every compatible feature of the relevant kind participates automatically.

  • Use pluss::null as to when you want matched cells to become missing.

resample¶

API Signature¶

DataFrameView resample(self, std::string_view time_feature, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> value_features, std::string_view freq, std::string_view op = "mean", std::int64_t step = 1, bool render = true) const

Parameters¶

time_feature : std::string_view Name of the Timeline or TimeIndex feature that defines the resampling, alignment, or calendar axis.

value_features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Feature name(s) to aggregate inside each resampling bin. Leave empty when you want PlussMic to infer compatible value features.

freq : std::string_view Bin or calendar frequency such as "1h", "D", "W", or "M".

op : std::string_view Bin reduction to compute in each time bucket.

Supported values:
- `count`: Count observed values within each bucket.
- `size`: Count rows within each bucket, including missing values.
- `sum`: Compute the numeric sum within each bucket.
- `mean`: Compute the arithmetic mean within each bucket.
- `min`: Compute the minimum within each bucket.
- `max`: Compute the maximum within each bucket.
- `first`: Take the first observed value within each bucket.
- `last`: Take the last observed value within each bucket.

step : std::int64_t Positive frequency multiplier. For example, 6 with hourly frequency means six-hour bins.

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

Returns¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

This is part of the time-aware surface and expects timeline or time-index semantics.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"ts", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_timeline({
        "2024-01-01T09:10:00Z",
        "2024-01-01T09:40:00Z",
        "2024-01-01T10:05:00Z",
    }))},
    {"load", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 15.0}))},
});

auto out = df.resample("ts", {"load"}, "1h", "mean", 1, false);

ts                   load
2024-01-01T09:00:00Z  15.0
2024-01-01T10:00:00Z  15.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • resample(...) groups rows into temporal bins and aggregates one value per bin and selected feature.

  • count ignores missing values, while size counts rows whether the value is missing or not.

  • For fixed frequencies, bins are anchored from the start of the local day rather than from the first observation timestamp.

  • Numeric reductions such as mean, sum, min, max, first, and last require numeric Series features.

reset_cases¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame reset_cases(self, std::string case_feature = "case") const

Parameters¶

case_feature : std::string Name to use for the restored case-axis feature when the current cases are materialized back into ordinary columns.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Materializes the current case axis as a normal feature, then restores the default positional cases 0..n-1.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto with_cases = df.set_cases("city", true);
auto out = with_cases.reset_cases("case");

with_cases.cases():
["Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"]

out.cases():
[0, 1, 2]

out.head():
id  sales  case
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

reshuffle¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame reshuffle(self, int axis = 0, std::optional<std::uint64_t> random_state = std::nullopt) const

Parameters¶

axis : int Axis selector. On DataFrame, 0 usually means rows/cases and 1 means features/columns.

random_state : std::optional<std::uint64_t> Optional seed used to make sampling or shuffling reproducible.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Applies reshuffle to the current DataFrame object. Use the example and output together to see which part of the object changes and which structure is preserved.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.reshuffle();

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • reshuffle(axis=0) permutes rows and keeps the feature order unchanged.

  • reshuffle(axis=1) permutes feature order and keeps the row order unchanged.

  • Pass random_state when you need deterministic shuffling for docs, tests, or reproducible data splits.

rolling¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame rolling(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<WindowSpec> specs, bool keep_input = true) const

Parameters¶

specs : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<WindowSpec> Window specs that define the output name, source feature, rolling operation, window width, and minimum observation policy.

keep_input : bool When true, the original features stay in the output and rolling features are appended. When false, only the derived rolling outputs are returned.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Computes rolling-window features and returns them as a derived frame.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.rolling({{.output = "sales_roll", .feature = "sales", .op = pluss::table::ThreadWindowOp::RollingMean, .window = 2, .min_periods = 1}}, false);

sales_roll
100.0
110.0
105.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • rolling(...) is the frame-level window-engineering route, so one call can derive several rolling outputs at once.

  • keep_input=true appends rolling outputs to the original frame, while keep_input=false returns only the engineered outputs.

  • Each WindowSpec controls the output name, source feature, operation, window width, and minimum observation rule.
