save_as¶

API Signatures¶

void save_as(self, std::string_view target_type, std::string_view filepath, const pluss::loader::Config& config = {}) const

void save_as(self, std::string_view target_type, std::string_view filepath, std::initializer_list<pluss::loader::ConfigEntry> config_entries) const

Parameters¶

target_type : std::string_view Format or target selector string used by this overload.

filepath : std::string_view File location to read from or write to. Use a neutral project path such as path/to/data.csv.

config : const pluss::loader::Config& Loader or saver configuration object. Use this when you want to pass a prebuilt option bundle instead of positional arguments.

config_entries : std::initializer_list<pluss::loader::ConfigEntry> Inline configuration entries used to build a lightweight loader configuration without naming a separate config object.

Returns¶

void Performs the side effect and returns no value.

What It Does¶

Writes the frame using the explicitly supplied output format selector rather than a dedicated saver overload.

Examples¶

Example 1. Save the frame with an explicit loader-config object.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

pluss::loader::Config config{};
df.save_as("json", "path/to/output.json", config);

saved: out.*

Example 2. Save the frame with inline configuration entries.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

df.save_as("json", "path/to/output.json", {"indent", 2});

saved: out.*

save_csv¶

API Signatures¶

void save_csv(self, std::string_view filepath) const

void save_csv(self, std::string_view filepath, bool add_cases, bool header = true, char sep = ',', std::string na_rep = "", std::optional<std::string> case_label = std::nullopt, std::optional<std::string> float_format = std::nullopt, char quotechar = '"', bool scalarquote = true, std::string line_terminator = "\n", char decimal = '.', std::string encoding = "utf-8") const

void save_csv(self, std::string_view filepath, const pluss::loader::Config& config) const

void save_csv(self, std::string_view filepath, std::initializer_list<pluss::loader::ConfigEntry> config_entries) const

Parameters¶

filepath : std::string_view File location to read from or write to. Use a neutral project path such as path/to/data.csv.

add_cases : bool When true, the current case axis is exported as its own column so row labels can be reconstructed when the file is loaded again.

header : bool Controls whether feature names are written to, or expected from, the file header row.

sep : char Column separator used for delimited text files such as CSV.

na_rep : std::string String written anywhere a null or missing value must be serialized.

case_label : std::optional<std::string> Optional column label to use for the exported case axis when add_cases=true.

float_format : std::optional<std::string> Optional numeric formatting string used when floating-point values are written to text output.

quotechar : char Quote character used when writing delimited text output.

doublequote : bool When true, embedded quote characters are escaped by doubling them in CSV-style output.

line_terminator : std::string Line ending written between serialized rows in text-based export.

decimal : char Decimal marker used when formatting floating-point output.

encoding : std::string Text encoding used when reading or writing text-based files.

config : const pluss::loader::Config& Loader or saver configuration object. Use this when you want to pass a prebuilt option bundle instead of positional arguments.

options : const pluss::loader::WriteCsvOptions& Typed loader, renderer, SQL, plotting, or policy options for this overload.

config_entries : std::initializer_list<pluss::loader::ConfigEntry> Inline configuration entries used to build a lightweight loader configuration without naming a separate config object.

Returns¶

void Performs the side effect and returns no value.

What It Does¶

Writes the frame to CSV. Set add_cases=true when you want the current case axis exported as a regular column so row labels survive the round trip.

Examples¶

Example 1. Save the frame using the simplest filepath-only overload.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

df.save_csv("path/to/output.csv");

saved: out.*

Example 2. Save the frame while controlling case-axis export and file-format details explicitly.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

df.save_csv("path/to/output.csv", true, true, ',', "NA", "case_id");

saved: out.*

Example 3. Save the frame with an explicit loader-config object.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

pluss::loader::Config config{};
df.save_csv("path/to/output.csv", config);

saved: out.*

Example 4. Save the frame with a typed writer-options object.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

pluss::loader::WriteCsvOptions options;
df.save_csv("path/to/output.csv", options);

saved: out.*

Example 5. Save the frame with inline configuration entries.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

df.save_csv("path/to/output.csv", {"indent", 2});

select_like¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame select_like(self, std::string_view needle, bool case_sensitive = true) const

Parameters¶

needle : std::string_view Substring token used to match feature names.

case_sensitive : bool When true, substring matching respects letter case. When false, feature names are matched case-insensitively.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Selects only the features whose names contain the requested substring.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"midterm_1", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({70.0, 80.0, 90.0}))},
    {"midterm_2", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({75.0, 85.0, 95.0}))},
    {"final_points", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({88.0, 91.0, 94.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.select_like("midterm");

midterm_1  midterm_2
70.0       75.0
80.0       85.0
90.0       95.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • select_like(...) filters feature names, not row values.

  • The output keeps the original row order and case axis unchanged.

  • Use this when you want schema-driven feature selection without listing every matching feature manually.

set¶

API Signatures¶

LetSlot set(self, std::string_view name)

LetSlots set(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> names)

LetSlots set(self, std::initializer_list<const char*> names)

LetSlots set(self, std::initializer_list<std::string_view> names)

Parameters¶

name : std::string_view Name used to identify the target object, field, feature, or slot for this overload.

names : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Collection of feature, slot, or stream names supplied in positional order.

Returns¶

LetSlot Value produced by this call.

LetSlots Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Opens an assignment helper so you can write df.set(...) = ... and replace or create features declaratively.

Examples¶

Example 1. Open the assignment helper for one feature name.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

df.set("profit") = pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({40.0, 35.0, 30.0}));

Example 2. Open the multi-feature assignment helper from a reusable feature-name range.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

df.set("profit") = pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({40.0, 35.0, 30.0}));

Example 3. Open the multi-feature assignment helper from inline C-string names.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

df.set({"profit", "cost"}) = {pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({40.0, 35.0, 30.0})), pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({60.0, 85.0, 60.0}))};

Example 4. Open the multi-feature assignment helper from inline string-view names.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

df.set({"profit", "cost"}) = {pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({40.0, 35.0, 30.0})), pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({60.0, 85.0, 60.0}))};

Parameters¶

names : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Collection of feature, slot, or stream names supplied in positional order.

Returns a new frame with one added or replaced feature.

Examples¶

Example 1. Add or replace several columns in one call.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.set_features(
    {"profit", "cost"},
    {
        pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({40.0, 35.0, 30.0})),
        pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({60.0, 85.0, 60.0})),
    });

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},

    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.set_features("profit", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({40.0, 35.0, 30.0})));

2   120.0  Tema    35.0

shift¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame shift(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> features, std::int64_t periods = 1) const

DataFrame shift(self, std::int64_t periods = 1) const

Parameters¶

features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Feature name(s) that select the target DataFrame columns for the operation.

periods : std::int64_t Number of rows to shift selected feature values. Positive values move values downward and introduce missing entries at the top; negative values move upward.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Applies shift to the current DataFrame object. Use the example and output together to see which part of the object changes and which structure is preserved.

Examples¶

Example 1. Shift only selected columns by a fixed number of rows.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.shift({"sales"}, 2);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Shift every compatible column by a fixed number of rows.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.shift(2);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

shift_time¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame shift_time(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> features, int periods, std::string_view freq) const

Parameters¶

features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Feature name(s) that select the target DataFrame columns for the operation.

periods : int Number of row or time steps to shift forward or backward. Positive values usually move data down or later; negative values move it up or earlier.

This is part of the time-aware surface and expects timeline or time-index semantics.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"ts", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_timeline({
        "2024-01-01T09:10:00Z",
        "2024-01-01T09:40:00Z",
        "2024-01-01T10:05:00Z",
    }))},
    {"load", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 15.0}))},
});

auto out = df.shift_time({"ts"}, 1, "hour");

ts
2024-01-01T10:10:00Z
2024-01-01T10:40:00Z
2024-01-01T11:05:00Z

Sorts rows by the current case axis rather than by a data feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({

    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},

});

auto with_cases = df.with_cases(pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"cs2", "cs0", "cs1"})));
auto out = with_cases.sort_cases(true, true);

with_cases.cases():
["cs2", "cs0", "cs1"]

out.cases():
["cs0", "cs1", "cs2"]

out.head():

1   100.0  Accra

sort_values¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame sort_values(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<ArrangeSpec> specs) const

DataFrame sort_values(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> features, bool ascending = true, bool nulls_last = true) const

Parameters¶

specs : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<ArrangeSpec> Collection of structured operation specs. Each element describes one requested summary, derive, transform, group, or placement rule depending on the method.

features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Feature names used as sort keys when you want the same ascending/null policy for every key.

ascending : bool When you use the simple feature-list overload, this one switch applies to every sort key. true sorts ascending and false sorts descending.

nulls_last : bool When true, null values are placed after observed values for every sort key in the simple overload. When false, nulls are placed first.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Reorders rows using one or more feature values as sort keys.

Examples¶

Example 1. Sort rows using explicit per-column sort specifications.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.sort_values({{.feature = "sales", .ascending = false}});

id  sales  city
2   120.0  Tema
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Sort rows using one shared ascending and null-order policy for every selected sort key.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.sort_values({"sales"}, false, true);

id  sales  city
2   120.0  Tema
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

sql¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrameSqlAccessor sql(self) const

DataFrameSqlAccessor sql(self, SqlOptions options) const

Parameters¶

options : SqlOptions SQL execution options such as engine or binding policy for the returned SQL accessor.

Returns¶

DataFrameSqlAccessor Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Use this when the transformation is easier to express as SQL than as a chained sequence of table verbs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Create the SQL accessor with default options and run a query immediately.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.sql().execute("SELECT id, sales FROM self WHERE sales > 95");

id  sales
1   100.0
2   120.0

Example 2. Create the SQL accessor with an explicit SQL options object before running a query.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

pluss::table::DataFrame::SqlOptions options;
auto sql = df.sql(options);
auto out = sql.execute("SELECT id, sales FROM self WHERE sales > 95");

id  sales
1   100.0
2   120.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • sql() returns the SQL accessor; it does not execute a statement by itself.

  • Call .execute(...) on the accessor when you want a result frame immediately.

  • Use prepare_sql(...) when the same query will be executed repeatedly with changing bindings.

std¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrameView std(self, bool render = true) const

Thread std(self, int axis, bool skipna = true) const

Thread std(self, std::int64_t axis, bool skipna = true) const

Parameters¶

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

axis : int Axis selector. On DataFrame, 0 usually means rows/cases and 1 means features/columns.

skipna : bool When true, missing values are skipped during the reduction. When false, missing state can affect the result.

Returns¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

Thread Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Computes per-feature standard deviations for the selected numeric features.

Examples¶

Example 1. Compute std for each numeric column in the frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.std(false);

feature  value
id       1.0
sales    15.275252317

Example 2. Compute std across rows instead of returning one summary value per numeric column.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.std(1, true);

feature  value
id       1.0
sales    15.275252317

Example 3. Compute std across rows instead of returning one summary value per numeric column.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.std(static_cast<std::int64_t>(1), true);

feature  value
id       1.0
sales    15.275252317

Practical Behavior¶

  • std(...) reduces the selected numeric features to one summary row.

  • Non-numeric features are skipped rather than coerced.

  • The output stays in DataFrame form, which makes these reducers easy to reuse in downstream frame pipelines.

stitch_on¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame stitch_on(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> left_features, const DataFrame& right, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> right_features = {}, std::string right_suffix = "_right") const

DataFrame stitch_on(self, std::initializer_list<std::string_view> left_features, const DataFrame& right, std::initializer_list<std::string_view> right_features = {}, std::string right_suffix = "_right") const

DataFrame stitch_on(self, std::string_view left_feature, const DataFrame& right, std::string_view right_feature = "", std::string right_suffix = "_right") const

Parameters¶

left_features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Key features on the left frame used to build a composite match key against the right frame.

right : const DataFrame& When true, intervals are right-closed. When false, they are left-closed and right-open.

right_features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Matching key features on the right frame. Leave empty to reuse the left feature names in the same order.

right_suffix : std::string Suffix added to right-hand feature names only when a non-key right feature would otherwise collide with an existing left feature name.

left_feature : std::string_view Key feature on the left frame used to match rows against the right frame.

right_feature : std::string_view Matching key feature on the right frame. Leave empty to reuse the left feature name.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Matches rows from two frames using key features and appends the matched features from the right-hand frame.

Examples¶

Example 1. Attach right-hand features by matching on one key feature.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"cost", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({60.0, 80.0, 55.0}))},
});

auto out = left.stitch_on("id", right, "id", "_right");

id  sales  cost
1   100.0  60.0
2   120.0  80.0
3    90.0  55.0

Example 2. Attach right-hand features by matching on several key features listed inline.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"cost", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({60.0, 80.0, 55.0}))},
});

auto out = left.stitch_on({"id"}, right, {"id"}, "_right");

id  sales  cost
1   100.0  60.0
2   120.0  80.0
3    90.0  55.0

Example 3. Attach right-hand features by matching on one key feature.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"cost", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({60.0, 80.0, 55.0}))},
});

auto out = left.stitch_on("id", right, "id", "_right");

id  sales  cost
1   100.0  60.0
2   120.0  80.0
3    90.0  55.0

Parameters¶

other : const DataFrame& Second frame, thread, or scalar operand supplied for binary combination, comparison, alignment, or join-style work.

This applies arithmetic across the compatible numeric payloads in the current object.

Examples¶

Example 1. Subtract each compatible numeric cell against another aligned frame.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2, 2, 4}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({110.0, 110.0, 100.0}))},
});

auto out = left.sub(right);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Subtract each compatible numeric cell against one broadcast scalar value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.sub(10);

id  sales  city
-9  90.0   Accra
-8  110.0  Tema
-7  80.0   Kumasi

T¶

tabelize¶

API Signatures¶

static DataFrame tabelize(const pluss::kindle::Catalog& catalog)

static DataFrame tabelize(const pluss::kindle::Catalog& catalog, const pluss::kindle::TabelizePolicy& policy)

Parameters¶

catalog : const pluss::kindle::Catalog& Catalog payload supplied to this overload.

policy : const pluss::kindle::TabelizePolicy& Policy object that changes the structural behavior of this overload.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Converts a Kindle Catalog into a tabular DataFrame, preserving stream alignment as rows.

Examples¶

Example 1. Convert a Kindle catalog into a frame with the default tabelization policy.

using namespace pluss::kindle::literals;
auto catalog = pluss::kindle::Catalog({"sales"_k = pluss::kindle::Stream(pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 30.0}))});
auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::tabelize(catalog);

sales
10.0
20.0
30.0

Example 2. Convert a Kindle catalog into a frame with an explicit tabelization policy.

using namespace pluss::kindle::literals;
auto catalog = pluss::kindle::Catalog({"sales"_k = pluss::kindle::Stream(pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 30.0}))});
pluss::kindle::TabelizePolicy policy;
auto out = pluss::table::DataFrame::tabelize(catalog, policy);

sales
10.0
20.0
30.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • tabelize(catalog) is the explicit bridge from Kindle stream collections into the DataFrame model.

  • Aligned streams become DataFrame features, and stream position becomes row position.

  • Use the policy overload when you want explicit tabelization rules instead of the defaults.

tail¶

API Signature¶

DataFrameView tail(self, std::int64_t n = 5, bool render = true) const

Parameters¶

n : std::int64_t Number of trailing rows to keep from the bottom of the frame.

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

Returns¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Returns the last n rows of the frame.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.tail(2, false);

id  sales  city
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • tail(n) preserves the original feature order and returns the last n rows.

  • If n is larger than the frame height, the whole frame is returned.

  • The returned object is a DataFrameView, so it behaves like a lightweight preview slice rather than a deep copy.

tally¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrameView tally(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> features, std::int64_t top_n = 0, bool dropna = true, bool render = true) const

DataFrameView tally(self, std::int64_t top_n = 0, bool dropna = true, bool render = true) const

DataFrameView tally(self, std::string_view feature, std::int64_t top_n = 0, bool dropna = true, bool render = true) const

Parameters¶

features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Feature name(s) that select the target DataFrame columns for the operation.

top_n : std::int64_t Optional cap on how many grouped rows to keep after sorting. Use 0 to keep every group.

dropna : bool When true, null grouping keys or null values are excluded where the method supports that policy. When false, null participates instead of being removed.

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

feature : std::string_view Name of the source feature used by the operation.

Returns¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Counts how many rows fall into each distinct value of the grouping feature.

Examples¶

Example 1. Count distinct combinations across several features.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Accra", "Tema", "Tema"}))},
    {"product", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"A", "B", "A", "B"}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0, 150.0}))},
});

auto out = df.tally({"city", "product"}, 5, true, false);

city    count
Accra   2
Tema    2

Example 2. Count distinct row groups using the default tally target.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Accra", "Tema", "Tema"}))},
    {"product", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"A", "B", "A", "B"}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0, 150.0}))},
});

auto out = df.tally(3, true, false);

city    count
Accra   2
Tema    2

Example 3. Count the distinct values in one named feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Accra", "Tema", "Tema"}))},
    {"product", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"A", "B", "A", "B"}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0, 150.0}))},
});

auto out = df.tally("city", 3, true, false);

city    count
Accra   2
Tema    2

title¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame title(self, std::string title) const

std::string title(self) const

Parameters¶

title : std::string Human-readable title stamp to attach to the returned frame.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

std::string Rendered string result.

What It Does¶

Gets the current frame title or returns a titled copy, depending on the overload.

Examples¶

Example 1. Return a titled copy of the current frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.title("sales_report");

out.title():
sales_report

out.head():
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Return a titled copy of the current frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto titled = df.title("sales_report");
auto out = titled.title();

sales_report

Practical Behavior¶

  • title() with no argument reads the current frame title.

  • title("...") returns a titled copy and leaves the source frame unchanged.

  • title_("...") mutates the current frame title in place.

top¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame top(self, std::string_view feature, std::int64_t n) const

Parameters¶

feature : std::string_view Name of the source feature used by the operation.

n : std::int64_t Number of rows, entries, or depth items to keep in the preview.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Returns the rows with the largest values in the selected feature.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.top("sales", 2);

id  sales  city
2   120.0  Tema
1   100.0  Accra

Practical Behavior¶

  • top(feature, n) sorts descending by the selected feature, keeps nulls last, then returns the first n rows.

  • The output rows stay aligned across every feature; this is not a single-column extraction.

  • Use bottom(...) when you want the smallest rows instead of the largest ones.

transform¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame transform(self, const std::function<Thread(const Thread&)>& fn) const

DataFrame transform(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<TransformSpec> specs) const

DataFrame transform(self, std::string_view feature, const std::function<Thread(const DataFrame&)>& fn) const

DataFrame transform(self, std::string_view feature, const std::function<Thread(const Thread&)>& fn) const

Parameters¶

fn : const std::function<Thread(const Thread&)>& Thread-to-thread or frame-to-thread transform function, depending on the overload. The returned thread must match the frame case count.

specs : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<TransformSpec> Collection of structured operation specs. Each element describes one requested summary, derive, transform, group, or placement rule depending on the method.

feature : std::string_view Target feature name to rewrite, or output feature name when you use the frame-aware derive overload.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Rewrites one feature, several features, or all features by applying a user function to each targeted thread.

Examples¶

Example 1. Rewrite every feature with the same thread-level transform.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.transform([](const pluss::table::Thread& thread) { return thread.kind() == pluss::table::ThreadKind::Series ? thread.clip(0.0, 110.0) : thread; });

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   110.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Rewrite one or more selected features with structured transform specs.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.transform({{.feature = "sales", .expr = [](const pluss::table::Thread& thread) { return thread.clip(0.0, 110.0); }}});

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   110.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 3. Derive or replace one feature by computing it from the full frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.transform("sales_plus_10", [](const pluss::table::DataFrame& frame) { return pluss::table::Thread(frame.features("sales").as_series().add(10.0)); });

id  sales  city    sales_plus_10
1   100.0  Accra   110.0
2   120.0  Tema    130.0
3    90.0  Kumasi  100.0

Example 4. Rewrite one named feature with a thread-level transform.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.transform("sales", [](const pluss::table::Thread& thread) { return thread.clip(0.0, 110.0); });

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   110.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • transform(fn) rewrites every feature with the same thread-level function.

  • transform(feature, thread_fn) rewrites one existing feature in place within the returned frame.

  • transform(feature, frame_fn) is the derive-style overload: it can create a new feature from the whole frame, as long as the returned thread matches the frame case count.

What It Does¶

Swaps rows and features so former feature names become row labels.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({

feature  row0   row1   row2
id       1      2      3
sales    100.0  120.0  90.0

truediv¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame truediv(self, const DataFrame& other) const

DataFrame truediv(self, scalar other) const

Parameters¶

other : const DataFrame& Scalar divisor or right-hand frame used for elementwise true division.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Applies elementwise true division to compatible numeric features.

Examples¶

Example 1. Divide each compatible numeric cell against another aligned frame.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2, 2, 4}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({110.0, 110.0, 100.0}))},
});

auto out = left.truediv(right);

id    sales
0.5   0.909091
1.0   1.090909
0.75  0.9

Example 2. Divide each compatible numeric cell against one broadcast scalar value.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.truediv(10);

id  sales  city
0.1  10.0  Accra
0.2  12.0  Tema
0.3   9.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • Scalar truediv(...) divides every compatible numeric cell by the supplied scalar.

  • Frame-vs-frame truediv(...) divides aligned numeric features row by row.

  • Non-numeric features pass through unchanged in the scalar form and are excluded from numeric combination work.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({

Example 2. Bind the time-series accessor by passing several feature names inline.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"ts", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_timeline({
        "2024-01-01T09:10:00Z",
        "2024-01-01T09:40:00Z",
        "2024-01-01T10:05:00Z",
    }))},
    {"load", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 15.0}))},
});

auto out = df.ts({"load"});

DataFrameTsAccessor(features=["load"])

Example 3. Bind the time-series accessor to one feature.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"ts", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_timeline({
        "2024-01-01T09:10:00Z",
        "2024-01-01T09:40:00Z",
        "2024-01-01T10:05:00Z",
    }))},
    {"load", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 15.0}))},
});

auto out = df.ts("load");

DataFrameTsAccessor(features=["load"])

Practical Behavior¶

  • ts(...) does not materialize a new DataFrame by itself; it returns the time-series accessor bound to the selected features.

  • Use the accessor when you want downstream resampling, lag blocks, rolling blocks, or calendar features on those bound features.

U¶

unify¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame unify(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> left_on, const DataFrame& right, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> right_on = {}, std::string_view how = "inner", std::string right_suffix = "_right", std::string_view validate = "many_to_many") const

DataFrame unify(self, std::initializer_list<std::string_view> left_on, const DataFrame& right, std::initializer_list<std::string_view> right_on = {}, std::string_view how = "inner", std::string right_suffix = "_right", std::string_view validate = "many_to_many") const

DataFrame unify(self, std::string_view left_on, const DataFrame& right, std::string_view right_on = "", std::string_view how = "inner", std::string right_suffix = "_right", std::string_view validate = "many_to_many") const

Parameters¶

left_on : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Key feature name(s) on the left frame used to match rows during unify(...).

right : const DataFrame& Right-hand frame whose rows are matched against the left frame by the requested key features.

right_on : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Key feature name(s) on the right frame used to match rows during unify(...). Leave empty to reuse the same names as left_on.

how : std::string_view Join mode for DataFrame::unify(...).

Supported values:
- `inner`: Keep only rows whose key values match on both sides.
- `left`: Preserve the left frame row order and row count, attaching right-hand matches where they exist.

right_suffix : std::string Suffix added to right-hand feature names only when a non-key right feature would otherwise collide with an existing left feature name.

validate : std::string_view Optional key-cardinality check for DataFrame::unify(...).

Supported values:
- `many_to_many`: Allow duplicate key values on both sides. This is the default.
- `one_to_one`: Require each key to appear at most once on both sides.
- `one_to_many`: Require unique keys on the left and allow duplicates on the right.
- `many_to_one`: Allow duplicates on the left and require unique keys on the right.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Joins two frames by key values. Use right_on="" when both frames use the same key name, how="left" to preserve left rows, and validate when you want duplicate-key checks such as "many_to_one".

Examples¶

Example 1. Join two frames on several key features supplied through a reusable string view.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"OrgDefinedId", pluss::make_note({"10", "20", "30"})},
    {"midterm", pluss::make_series({71, 82, 93})},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"OrgDefinedId", pluss::make_note({"20", "30"})},
    {"Final Points Grade", pluss::make_series({88, 99})},
});

auto out = left.unify(
    "OrgDefinedId",
    right,
    "",
    "left",
    "_right",
    "many_to_one"
);

OrgDefinedId  midterm  Final Points Grade
10            71       null
20            82       88
30            93       99

Example 2. Join two frames on several key features listed inline.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"course", pluss::make_note({"STAT200", "STAT200", "STAT300"})},
    {"OrgDefinedId", pluss::make_note({"10", "20", "30"})},
    {"midterm", pluss::make_series({71, 82, 93})},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"course_code", pluss::make_note({"STAT200", "STAT300"})},
    {"Username", pluss::make_note({"20", "30"})},
    {"Final Points Grade", pluss::make_series({88, 99})},
});

auto out = left.unify(
    {"course", "OrgDefinedId"},
    right,
    {"course_code", "Username"},
    "inner",
    "_right",
    "one_to_one"
);

course   OrgDefinedId  midterm  course_code  Username  Final Points Grade
STAT200  20            82       STAT200      20        88
STAT300  30            93       STAT300      30        99

Example 3. Join two frames on one key feature name.

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"OrgDefinedId", pluss::make_note({"10", "20", "30"})},
    {"midterm", pluss::make_series({71, 82, 93})},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"OrgDefinedId", pluss::make_note({"20", "30"})},
    {"Final Points Grade", pluss::make_series({88, 99})},
});

auto out = left.unify(
    "OrgDefinedId",
    right,
    "",
    "left",
    "_right",
    "many_to_one"
);

OrgDefinedId  midterm  Final Points Grade
10            71       null
20            82       88
30            93       99

Join Semantics¶

  • unify(...) matches rows by key values, not by current row order.

  • how="left" preserves the left frame row order and row count, while how="inner" keeps matched rows only.

  • When right-hand non-key names collide with left-hand names, right_suffix is applied only to the right-hand collisions.

unique¶

API Signature¶

bool unique(self) const

Parameters¶

None

Returns¶

bool Boolean status or membership result.

What It Does¶

Reports whether the object satisfies the uniqueness constraint expected by its model, such as distinct labels or keys.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},

});

auto out = df.unique();

true

unique_cases¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame unique_cases(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> features = {}) const

Parameters¶

features : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<std::string_view> Optional feature subset used to decide which rows count as duplicates. Leave empty to compare the full row payload.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Keeps only the first occurrence of each case label and drops later duplicates.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"campus", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"North", "North", "West"}))},
    {"student", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Ada", "Kojo", "Esi"}))},
    {"score", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({88.0, 91.0, 84.0}))},
});

auto out = df.unique_cases({"campus"});

campus  student  score
North   Ada      88.0
West    Esi      84.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • unique_cases(features) keeps only the first row for each distinct key combination defined by features.

  • With no feature list, the full row payload is used as the duplicate key.

  • This is the row-filtering companion to repeated_cases(...).

unsqueeze¶

API Signatures¶

Atlas unsqueeze(self) const

Atlas unsqueeze(self, const Thread& depth_labels) const

Parameters¶

depth_labels : const Thread& Single depth label to attach to the one-frame atlas produced by unsqueeze(...).

Returns¶

Atlas Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Promotes the frame into a depth-1 Atlas so it can participate in multi-frame workflows.

Examples¶

Example 1. Lift one frame into a one-layer atlas.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.unsqueeze();

frame0:
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Lift one frame into a one-layer atlas.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto labels = pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"train"}));
auto out = df.unsqueeze(labels);

depth labels:
["train"]

frame0:
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • unsqueeze() wraps one frame into a depth-1 Atlas.

  • The depth_labels overload lets you attach exactly one depth label to that one-frame atlas.

  • This is useful when downstream APIs expect atlas depth even though you currently have only one frame.

update¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame update(self, const DataFrame& other, bool overwrite = true) const

Parameters¶

other : const DataFrame& Second frame, thread, or scalar operand supplied for binary combination, comparison, alignment, or join-style work.

overwrite : bool When true, matching values from the right-hand side overwrite existing left-hand values during update-style operations.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Overlays matching features from another frame onto this frame using aligned cases.

Examples¶

auto left = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
});
auto right = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"cost", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({60.0, 80.0, 55.0}))},
});

auto out = left.update(right);

id  sales  cost
1   100.0  60.0
2   120.0  80.0
3    90.0  55.0

V¶

var¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrameView var(self, bool render = true) const

Thread var(self, int axis, bool skipna = true) const

Thread var(self, std::int64_t axis, bool skipna = true) const

Parameters¶

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

axis : int Axis selector. On DataFrame, 0 usually means rows/cases and 1 means features/columns.

skipna : bool When true, missing values are skipped during the reduction. When false, missing state can affect the result.

Returns¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

Thread Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Computes per-feature variances for the selected numeric features.

Examples¶

Example 1. Compute var for each numeric column in the frame.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.var(false);

feature  value
id       1.0
sales    233.333333333

Example 2. Compute var across rows instead of returning one summary value per numeric column.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.var(1, true);

feature  value
id       1.0
sales    233.333333333

Example 3. Compute var across rows instead of returning one summary value per numeric column.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"a", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0}))},
    {"b", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, 5.0}))},
});

auto out = df.var(static_cast<std::int64_t>(1), true);

feature  value
id       1.0
sales    233.333333333

Practical Behavior¶

  • var(...) reduces the selected numeric features to one summary row.

  • Non-numeric features are skipped rather than coerced.

  • The output stays in DataFrame form, which makes these reducers easy to reuse in downstream frame pipelines.

view¶

API Signature¶

DataFrameView view(self, std::int64_t start, std::int64_t stop, bool render = true) const

Parameters¶

start : std::int64_t Slice start position. Negative values count backward from the end of the frame.

stop : std::int64_t Slice stop position. Negative values count backward from the end, and -1 includes the last row.

render : bool When true, the returned view can auto-render in temporary terminal contexts. Pass false when you want explicit output control.

Returns¶

DataFrameView Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Returns a lightweight row view of the requested slice.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.view(0, 2, false);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema

Slice Semantics¶

  • view(start, stop) behaves like a positional row slice [start, stop).

  • Negative start or stop values count backward from the end of the frame.

  • Unlike slice(...), view(...) returns a DataFrameView wrapper intended for lightweight inspection.

W¶

where¶

API Signatures¶

DataFrame where(self, const pluss::Series& bool_mask) const

DataFrame where(self, const Thread& bool_mask) const

Parameters¶

bool_mask : const pluss::Series& Boolean row mask. Rows where the mask is true are kept; rows where it is false are dropped.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Keeps only the rows where the supplied boolean mask is true.

Examples¶

Example 1. Filter rows using an explicit boolean Series mask.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto mask = pluss::make_series({true, false, true}, pluss::codem::ScalarType::Bool);
auto out = df.where(mask);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

Example 2. Filter rows using a boolean mask built from an existing frame expression.

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto mask = df.features("sales") >= 95.0;
auto out = df.where(mask);

id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
3    90.0  Kumasi

Practical Behavior¶

  • where(mask) keeps rows where the boolean mask is true and drops the rest.

  • The mask length must match the frame case count exactly.

  • Use put(...) when you want masked replacement inside one feature instead of masked row filtering.

window¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame window(self, pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<WindowSpec> specs, bool keep_input = true) const

Parameters¶

specs : pluss::msharp::RangeView::Of<WindowSpec> Collection of structured operation specs. Each element describes one requested summary, derive, transform, group, or placement rule depending on the method.

keep_input : bool When true, the original input features are preserved and engineered window outputs are appended. When false, only the engineered outputs are returned.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Computes one or more window-based features such as rolling means over selected columns.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto out = df.window({{.output = "sales_roll", .feature = "sales", .op = pluss::table::ThreadWindowOp::RollingMean, .window = 2, .min_periods = 1}}, false);

sales_roll
100.0
110.0
105.0

Practical Behavior¶

  • window(...) engineers one or more derived features from rolling/window operations described by WindowSpec.

  • keep_input=false returns only the engineered outputs, which is useful for model-matrix style pipelines.

  • rolling(...) is the alias that delegates to the same frame-level implementation.

with_cases¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame with_cases(self, const Thread& cases) const

Parameters¶

cases : const Thread& Case-label thread to attach to the current object.

Returns¶

DataFrame Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Replaces the current case axis with the supplied thread. The row values stay in the same order, but later case-aware operations now use the new labels.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto cases = pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"cs0", "cs1", "cs2"}));
auto out = df.with_cases(cases);

df.cases():
[0, 1, 2]

out.cases():
["cs0", "cs1", "cs2"]

out.head():
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi

with_cases_¶

API Signature¶

DataFrame& with_cases_(self, const Thread& cases)

Parameters¶

cases : const Thread& Case-label thread to attach to the current object.

Returns¶

DataFrame& Value produced by this call.

What It Does¶

Replaces the current case axis in place. The row values stay in the same order, but later case-aware operations now use the new labels.

Examples¶

auto df = pluss::table::DataFrame({
    {"id", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}))},
    {"sales", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_series({100.0, 120.0, 90.0}))},
    {"city", pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"Accra", "Tema", "Kumasi"}))},
});

auto cases = pluss::table::Thread(pluss::make_note({"cs0", "cs1", "cs2"}));
df.with_cases_(cases);

df.cases():
["cs0", "cs1", "cs2"]

df.head():
id  sales  city
1   100.0  Accra
2   120.0  Tema
3    90.0  Kumasi
